name: Cranial bone graft for nasal dorsum

lead:
Cranial (calvarial) bone grafting uses bone from the outer skull to restore or heighten the nasal dorsum, the bridge of the nose. It is one of the options surgeons use when the bridge has collapsed or needs strong structural support.
Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article lists cranial bone with rib and ear cartilage as grafts that can restore a collapsed bridge, and says patients' own tissue is preferred to artificial implants for lower rejection and complication rates.

paras: It is done by a surgeon during rhinoplasty: bone is harvested from the skull and shaped to the bridge. Bone can also come from the hip or rib.
Surgery risks apply, and the harvest creates a second surgical site on the skull. Healing in the nose can be unpredictable.

angle.text: It reshapes the nose by adding a rigid, own-tissue structure to the bridge.

lead: A cranial or calvarial bone graft takes bone from the patient's skull to rebuild the nasal dorsum.[1] According to the Wikipedia rhinoplasty article, rib cartilage, ear cartilage or cranial bone can restore a collapsed bridge's anatomy, and own-tissue grafts are preferred over artificial implants for lower rejection and complication rates.[1]

Surgeons choose between septal, ear (concha) and rib cartilage, bone from the skull, hip or rib cage, or synthetic implants when autologous grafts are unavailable.[1] For appearance, the goal is a straighter, higher or better-supported bridge.
infobox: Rib or ear cartilage, hip bone, implants

paras: Cartilage usually comes from the septum, and if insufficient from the rib or ear; bone comes from the cranium, hip or rib; synthetic implants are used when no autologous graft is available.[1]
Nasal healing can be unpredictable, smoking impairs it, and revision cases often need rib or ear cartilage.[1]
